docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: This is my individual datasheet site for Project Aurora, a smart medication holder built by Team 102. It documents my subsystem from the block diagram through parts selection, schematic, and power budget.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Project Aurora helps a user take their medication on time. Four connected boards share the job: a weight board detects when a dose is removed, a cap board detects when the bottle is opened, an environment board watches storage temperature and light, and a hub board keeps the schedule and gives reminders. The boards talk to each other over 8-pin ribbon cables. See the team website for the full system.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
I am designing the Reminder & Alerts hub board (Member C). It keeps the dose schedule with a real-time clock, alerts the user with a speaker and a high-brightness LED, shows status on three LEDs, and connects to the three sensing boards.

Datasheet sections:

  • Block Diagram: how my board is laid out, its power supplies, parts, and microcontroller pin use

Team 102 – Project Aurora · Taylor Callo · Member C: Reminder & Alerts (Hub)

My board is the hub of our system. It keeps the dose schedule with a real-time clock, gives sound and light reminders, and talks to the three sensing boards (Weight, Cap / Lid, Storage Environment) over three 8-pin ribbon cables.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
Team 102 – Project Aurora · Taylor Callo · Member C: Reminder & Alerts (Hub)

This page compares three real options for every major part on my Reminder & Alerts hub board, and explains which one I picked and why. My hub board keeps track of when each dose is due using a clock chip, warns the user with a speaker and a bright LED when it is time, and gets its power from a 9 V wall adapter that goes through a 5 V regulator. The assignment says not to include the microcontroller (it was picked for us), resistors, capacitors, buttons, or plain LEDs, so those are left out.

All prices are for buying 1 part, in US dollars, checked on 10/14/2026. My board will be cut on the Peralta lab's PCB mill and soldered by hand, so I picked parts with pins that go through the board (through-hole) or parts that are still easy to solder by hand.

docs.text: Part Subsystem Choice Cost Audio amplifier Reminder & Alerts (Hub) TI LM386N-1/NOPB $1.18 Speaker Reminder & Alerts (Hub) Same Sky CMS-40558N-L152 $5.88 Real-time clock Reminder & Alerts (Hub) Microchip MCP7940N-I/P $0.92 RTC backup battery Reminder & Alerts (Hub) Panasonic CR2032 + Keystone 1066 holder $1.48 Alert LED switch Reminder & Alerts (Hub) Alpha & Omega AO3400A $0.52 Alert LED Reminder & Alerts (Hub) Kingbright WP7113SEC/J3 $0.76 5 V regulator Power (Hub board) STMicroelectronics L7805CV $0.50 Wall adapter Power (Hub board) Triad Magnetics WSU090-2000 $12.43

docs.title: 1. Audio Amplifier — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
The PIC sends a beeping signal (PWM) out of pin RC2, but that signal is too weak to play through a speaker by itself. The amplifier makes the signal stronger so it can drive the 8 Ω speaker, using power from the 5 V rail.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Texas Instruments LM386N-1/NOPB (DIP-8)$1.18/eachLM386N-1 at DigiKey • Its pins go through the board (DIP-8), so it is easy to solder by hand on the milled board• Works on anything from 4 V to 12 V, so it can plug right into my 5 V rail• The gain (how much it boosts the signal) is already set to 20 inside the chip, so I only need a few extra parts• It is a very popular chip, so there are lots of example circuits and help online • Needs a big (about 250 µF) capacitor between the chip and the speaker, which takes up board space• Only puts out about 0.25 W at 5 V, which is loud enough for a reminder beep but not very loud• Uses 4–8 mA of power even when it is not making any sound Option 2. Nisshinbo NJM2113D (DIP-8)$0.96/eachNJM2113D at DigiKey • Its pins go through the board and it is the cheapest of the three• Drives the speaker from both sides, so it does not need the big output capacitor• Has a mute pin the PIC can use to turn it almost fully off between alerts, saving power • The datasheet does not say how much power it can give an 8 Ω speaker (it is rated for 32 Ω), so I can't be sure it will be loud enough• Neither speaker wire can go to ground, because of the way it drives the speaker• There are far fewer examples online than for the LM386 Option 3. Diodes Inc. PAM8302AADCR (SOIC-8, class-D)$0.67/eachPAM8302AADCR at DigiKey • By far the loudest option, up to 2.5 W from 5 V• Very efficient (up to 88%), so it barely gets warm• Has a built-in off switch plus protection if the speaker wires short or it gets too hot • Surface-mount only (the chip sits on top of the board), which is harder to solder on a milled board• The way it switches on and off very fast can add electrical noise near the sensor signals coming from the other boards• Neither speaker wire can go to ground

Choice: Option 1, Texas Instruments LM386N-1/NOPB

Rationale: I picked the LM386N-1 because it is a through-hole chip that runs right off my 5 V rail and only needs a few extra parts, which keeps my milled board simple. About 0.25 W is loud enough to hear a reminder beep inside a home, and the chip is in stock with tons of help online if I run into problems. The PAM8302A is louder and more efficient, but it is surface-mount only and I don't need that much volume for a short beep. The NJM2113D was close, but its datasheet doesn't say how it works with an 8 Ω speaker, so I couldn't be sure it would drive mine.

docs.title: 2. Speaker — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
Plays the beep that tells the user it is time to take a dose. It needs to be 8 Ω and able to handle at least the 0.25 W the LM386 can send it.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Same Sky CMS-40558N-L152 (40 mm, 8 Ω)$5.88/eachCMS-40558N-L152 at DigiKey • Rated for 0.5 W (1 W max), which is double what the amplifier can send, so it won't get damaged• Very loud for its size (90 dB), so the beep is easy to hear even at low power• Comes with wires already attached, so it can plug into a header on my board• Thin (5.5 mm) and in stock at DigiKey • At 40 mm across, it is the biggest of the three options• Not good at low sounds (below about 500 Hz), so the beep needs to be a higher pitch Option 2. PUI Audio AS02808MR-LW152-R (28 mm, 8 Ω)$4.82/each (Mouser)AS02808MR-LW152-R at DigiKey • Smaller (28 mm), so it is easier to fit inside the medication holder• Rated for 1 W and very loud (95 dB)• Comes with wires already attached • I couldn't confirm DigiKey has it in stock, so I might have to order it from Mouser separately• A smaller speaker sounds thinner and less full Option 3. Visaton K 28 WPC BL (28 mm, 8 Ω)$7.24/eachK 28 WPC BL at DigiKey • Handles the most power (1 W rated, 2 W max), so there is lots of room for error• Has mounting tabs, so it is easy to screw into the enclosure• Good-quality brand that plays a wide range of sounds (300 Hz–20 kHz) • The most expensive of the three• Only has solder tabs, so I would have to solder wires onto it myself

Choice: Option 1, Same Sky CMS-40558N-L152

Rationale: I picked this speaker because it is the right resistance (8 Ω), it can handle twice the power my amplifier puts out, and it is loud, so the reminder beep will be easy to hear without pushing the amplifier hard. The wires that come attached plug straight into a 2-pin header on my board, and it is in stock at DigiKey with my other parts. Its 40 mm size still fits inside the hub's case.

docs.title: 3. Real-Time Clock — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
Keeps track of the time and date so the hub knows when each dose is due, even if the board loses power. It can also set an alarm that tells the PIC "it's time" on pin RB2. It talks to the PIC using I²C on pins RC3 and RC4.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Microchip MCP7940N-I/P (DIP-8)$0.92/eachMCP7940N-I/P at DigiKey • Works on 1.8–5.5 V, so it runs fine on the PIC's 3.3 V• Its pins go through the board, so it is easy to solder• Has two built-in alarms and an alarm pin to tell the PIC when a dose is due• Cheapest option, and only uses 1.2 µA from the backup battery • Needs a separate 32.768 kHz crystal and two small capacitors to keep time• Only as accurate as the crystal (can drift about 1 minute per month unless adjusted)• The code has to turn on its clock and its battery backup at startup Option 2. Analog Devices DS1307+ (DIP-8)$6.94/each (Mouser)DS1307+ at DigiKey • Its pins go through the board• Very well known, with lots of example code• Uses very little power from the backup battery • Only runs on 5 V, so I would have to be careful connecting it to the 3.3 V PIC• Has no alarms, so the PIC would have to keep checking the time over and over• Slower communication, also needs a crystal, and costs about 7× more Option 3. Analog Devices DS3231SN# (SOIC-16)$19.05/eachDS3231SN# at DigiKey • Extremely accurate (drifts about 1 minute per year)• Crystal is built in, so there is nothing extra to wire up• Has two alarms and works at 3.3 V • Costs about 20× more than the MCP7940N• Surface-mount only• Much more accurate than a pill reminder needs

Choice: Option 1, Microchip MCP7940N-I/P

Rationale: I picked the MCP7940N because it is the only option that has through-hole pins, works at 3.3 V, and has alarms, so it can wake up the hub when a dose is due without the PIC constantly checking. It is also the cheapest and is made by Microchip, the same company as our microcontroller. Adding a small crystal is a small extra step, and the chip can be adjusted in code to fix the crystal's drift. The DS3231 is more accurate, but a pill reminder only needs to be right within about a minute, which isn't worth 20× the price and a harder-to-solder chip.

docs.title: 4. RTC Backup Battery — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
A small coin battery that keeps the clock running when the wall adapter is unplugged, so the dose schedule isn't lost.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Panasonic CR2032 (3 V, 225 mAh)$0.36/each + $1.12 holder → $0.36/each (holder: 1.12 USD)CR2032 at DigiKey · Keystone 1066 holder • 225 mAh lasts for decades at the clock's tiny 1.2 µA draw• Cheapest, and sold almost everywhere, so a user can easily replace it• Has a through-hole holder that fits my milled board • The 20 mm holder takes up some board space• Not rechargeable Option 2. Renata CR2032 MFR.IB (3 V, 225 mAh)$0.44/each (Mouser)Renata CR2032 at Mouser • Same size and capacity as Option 1• Loses less than 1% of its charge per year while sitting• Well-documented Swiss brand • Costs a little more• I could only confirm it at Mouser, not DigiKey Option 3. Panasonic CR1220 (3 V, 35 mAh)$1.02/each (Mouser) + $1.22 holderCR1220 at Mouser • Small (12 mm), so the battery and holder save board space• 35 mAh still lasts years at 1.2 µA • Only about 1/6 the capacity of a CR2032• Costs about 3× more• Harder for a user to find a replacement

Choice: Option 1, Panasonic CR2032 in a Keystone 1066 holder

Rationale: At the clock's tiny 1.2 µA draw, a 225 mAh CR2032 would last longer than its own ~10-year shelf life, so the user should never need to think about it. It is the cheapest option, fits in a through-hole holder on my board, and is the most common coin battery, so it is easy to replace if ever needed.

docs.title: 5. Alert LED Switch (MOSFET) — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
Works like an electronic switch. It lets PIC pin RC5 (3.3 V) turn the bright alert LED on and off using power from the 5 V rail, so the LED's current doesn't flow through the PIC itself.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Alpha & Omega AO3400A (SOT-23)$0.52/eachAO3400A at DigiKey • The datasheet guarantees it turns fully on with only 2.5 V, so the PIC's 3.3 V is plenty• Can handle up to 5.7 A, so I could switch to a much brighter LED later• The cheapest of the three • The small 3-pin package takes some care to solder by hand• Fake copies with the same name exist, so I need to buy it from DigiKey Option 2. onsemi 2N7000 (TO-92)$1.23/each (Mouser)2N7000 at DigiKey • Its pins go through the board, so it is the easiest to solder• Very common and well-known part • Might need up to 3 V just to start turning on, so it may barely work from the PIC's 3.3 V• Can only handle 200 mA• Leaves no room to upgrade to a brighter LED Option 3. Infineon IRLZ44NPBF (TO-220)$1.80/each (Mouser)IRLZ44NPBF at DigiKey • Its pins go through the board, so it is easy to solder• Turns on at a low voltage (1–2 V) and wastes very little power when on • The datasheet only guarantees full performance at 4 V or more, not at 3.3 V• Big package for such a small LED• The most expensive of the three

Choice: Option 1, Alpha & Omega AO3400A

Rationale: I picked the AO3400A because it is the only option the datasheet guarantees will fully turn on from a 3.3 V pin, so the alert LED will always turn on all the way when the PIC tells it to. Its pins are 0.95 mm apart, which is wider than the Peralta mill's 0.8 mm minimum, so I can still solder it by hand with care. I looked at through-hole parts, but the 2N7000 might not turn on from 3.3 V, and the IRLZ44N isn't guaranteed at 3.3 V and is much bigger than I need.

docs.title: 6. High-Brightness Alert LED — Reminder & Alerts (Hub)
docs.text:
The light that tells the user a dose is due. It needs to be bright enough to notice from across a room. It is turned on and off by the AO3400A using power from the 5 V rail. (The three small Ready/Taken/Error status LEDs are regular LEDs, so they are not listed here.)

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Kingbright WP7113SEC/J3 (5 mm red)$0.76/each (Mouser)WP7113SEC/J3 at DigiKey • Very bright: 15,000 mcd at 20 mA• Red clearly means "pay attention"• Its pins go through the board and it only needs one resistor (about 150 Ω) to run on 5 V• Only uses 20 mA, which keeps the power budget small • The light shines in a narrow 20° beam, so it is easiest to see from the front• Can't be made much brighter (30 mA max) Option 2. Cree C503B-WAN-CBBDB231 (5 mm white)$0.28/each (Mouser)C503B-WAN at Mouser • The brightest 5 mm option: 20,000–34,000 mcd at 20 mA• The cheapest option• Its pins go through the board • Very narrow 15° beam, so it is hard to see from the side• White light doesn't say "alert" as clearly as red• Only 25 mA max Option 3. Cree XLamp XP-G3 star LED (white)$11.40/each (Mouser)XP-G3 star LED at Mouser • Extremely bright (about 165 lumens) with a wide 125° beam• Can be seen from anywhere in the room • Needs 350 mA, which would add about 1.75 W of heat to my 5 V regulator• Mounted on a metal star board, so it has to be wired by hand and needs a heatsink• Costs about 15× more than a 5 mm LED

Choice: Option 1, Kingbright WP7113SEC/J3

Rationale: I picked this LED because it is bright enough to notice across a room, and red clearly tells the user it is time for a dose. At only 20 mA it keeps my 5 V regulator cool, and it is a cheap through-hole part. The XP-G3 star LED is much brighter, but its 350 mA draw would make the regulator way too hot. Since the LED is controlled by the AO3400A switch, I could swap in the star LED later without changing the board.

docs.title: 7. 5 V Voltage Regulator — Power (Hub board)
docs.text:
Turns the 9 V from the wall adapter into a steady 5 V for the Curiosity Nano, the amplifier, and the alert LED. The course requires a linear regulator.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. STMicroelectronics L7805CV (TO-220)$0.50/eachL7805CV at DigiKey • It is a linear regulator, so it meets the course rule• Can supply up to 1.5 A, about 3× the most my board needs• Works with small, cheap capacitors (0.33 µF in, 0.1 µF out)• The cheapest option, with built-in protection if it overheats or shorts • Needs at least 7 V coming in (my 9 V adapter is fine)• Turns the extra 4 V into heat, so it needs a heatsink when everything is on Option 2. Texas Instruments LM2940CT-5.0/NOPB (TO-220)$1.94/eachLM2940CT-5.0 at DigiKey • Keeps working even if the input drops to about 5.5 V• Protected if the power is hooked up backwards• It is a linear regulator, so it meets the course rule • Needs a large output capacitor of a specific type, or it can become unstable• Makes the same amount of heat as the 7805, because the heat depends on 9 V − 5 V• Uses more power itself and costs about 4× more Option 3. RECOM R-78E5.0-1.0 (switching)$3.97/eachR-78E5.0-1.0 at DigiKey • About 92% efficient, so it barely gets warm and needs no heatsink• Same pin layout as a 7805, so it can drop right in • It is a switching regulator, not linear, so it does not meet the course rule• Adds a small ripple to the output that could add noise to sensor readings• Costs about 8× more

Choice: Option 1, STMicroelectronics L7805CV (with a clip-on TO-220 heatsink)

Rationale: I picked the L7805CV because it meets the course's linear-regulator rule, can supply 1.5 A when my board only needs about 0.5 A, and works with small, cheap capacitors. The LM2940's ability to work at a lower input voltage doesn't help me since I have a 9 V adapter, and it needs a special output capacitor. Both linear regulators make the same heat, so I will add a clip-on heatsink (worked out in my Power Budget). The switching regulator would stay cool, but the course doesn't allow it.

docs.title: 8. External Power Supply — Power (Hub board)
docs.text:
Plugs into the wall and gives 9 V DC to the board through the PJ-102AH barrel jack. It needs a 5.5 × 2.1 mm plug with positive in the center, and must supply at least the board's ~0.5 A worst case.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Triad Magnetics WSU090-2000 (9 V, 2 A)$12.43/each (Mouser)WSU090-2000 at Mouser • Supplies 2 A, about 4× the most my board needs• Plugs straight into the wall• Has the right size plug with positive in the center• The cheapest of the three • Not many in stock, and more take a long time to arrive• A very similar "-R" version has the polarity flipped, so I have to make sure not to order that one Option 2. MEAN WELL GST18A09-P1J (9 V, 2 A)$14.10/each (Mouser)GST18A09-P1J at Mouser • High-quality brand with a 2 A output• Has the right size plug with positive in the center • It is a desktop power brick, not a wall plug, so it needs a separate AC cord• Low stock at both Mouser and DigiKey Option 3. CUI SWI12-9-N-P5 (9 V, 1.2 A)$17.59/each (Mouser)SWI12-9-N-P5 at Mouser • Lots in stock (800+)• Plugs into the wall and has the right plug • The most expensive• Supplies the least current (1.2 A), the least room for error

Choice: Option 1, Triad Magnetics WSU090-2000

Rationale: I picked this adapter because it is the cheapest, plugs right into the wall, and supplies 2 A, which is way more than my worst case of about 0.52 A (with the 25% safety margin). It has the right plug for my barrel jack. I will make sure to order the WSU090-2000 and not the "-R" version, which has the polarity flipped and would send power backwards into the board. If it goes out of stock, the CUI adapter is my backup.

docs.title: Power Budget
docs.text:
Team 102 – Project Aurora · Taylor Callo · Member C: Reminder & Alerts (Hub)

This page checks that my wall adapter and voltage regulators can power everything on my hub board at the same time, with a 25% safety margin on top. It follows the course power budget template: each part that uses power is put on one power rail, each rail's total is multiplied by 1.25, and then I check that the regulators and wall adapter still have current left over. All currents are the maximum values from each part's datasheet unless I say it is an estimate.

docs.title: +5V Power Rail
docs.text:
+5V Power Rail Component Name Part Number Supply Voltage Range Qty. Absolute Maximum Current (mA) Total Current (mA) Unit Audio Amplifier LM386N-1/NOPB 4 V – 12 V 1 258 258 mA Alert LED WP7113SEC/J3 5 V rail (150 Ω resistor) 1 20 20 mA Curiosity Nano (powers the +3.3V rail) DM164150 5 V (VBUS) 1 130.4 130.4 mA Subtotal 408.4 mA Safety Margin 25% Total Current Required on +5V Rail 510.5 mA Regulator +5V Linear Regulator L7805CV 7 V – 35 V 1 1500 1500 mA Total Remaining Current Available on +5V Rail 989.5 mA
  • LM386: uses up to 8 mA just being on, plus up to 250 mA at the loudest point of the beep going to the 8 Ω speaker.
  • Curiosity Nano: its built-in 3.3 V regulator gets its power from this 5 V rail, so it pulls the same current as everything on the +3.3V rail below.
  • Not listed (per the assignment): the AO3400A switch (it turns the LED on and off but uses almost no power itself), the speaker (its current is already counted in the LM386 line), and resistors and capacitors.

Absolute Maximum Current (mA) Total Current (mA) Unit Microcontroller + debugger PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 1.8 V – 5.5 V 1 100 100 mA Real-Time Clock MCP7940N-I/P 1.8 V – 5.5 V 1 0.4 0.4 mA Status LEDs Standard indicator LEDs 3.3 V rail 3 10 30 mA Subtotal 130.4 mA Safety Margin 25% Total Current Required on +3.3V Rail 163.0 mA Regulator +3.3V Regulator (built into the Nano) MIC5353 2.6 V – 6 V 1 500 500 mA Total Remaining Current Available on +3.3V Rail 337.0 mA
  • Microcontroller: 100 mA is my estimate for the PIC running at full speed plus the Nano's built-in programmer/debugger. The Curiosity Nano guide doesn't give one single maximum number.
  • Clock: uses at most 0.4 mA while talking to the PIC, and only 1.2 µA the rest of the time.
  • Status LEDs: these are regular LEDs. I listed them anyway because together they add 30 mA, which isn't tiny.
  • Ribbon-cable signals going to the other boards use less than 0.1 mA total, so they are not listed.

docs.title: External Power Source
docs.text:
External Power Source 1 Component Name Part Number Supply Voltage Range Output Voltage Absolute Maximum Current (mA) Total Current (mA) Unit Power Source 1 Selection Plug-in Wall Supply Triad Magnetics WSU090-2000 100 – 240 VAC +9 V 2000 2000 mA Power Rails Connected to External Power Source 1 +5V Regulator L7805CV 7 V – 35 V +5 V 1500 1500 mA Total Remaining Current Available on External Power Source 1 500 mA
  • Even if the 5 V regulator used its full 1.5 A, the adapter would still have 500 mA left over, so the remaining current is positive and the adapter is big enough.
  • The +3.3V regulator doesn't connect to the adapter directly. It gets its power from the +5V rail, so its current is already counted there.
  • The adapter's plug is 5.5 × 2.1 mm with positive in the center, which fits the board's Same Sky PJ-102AH barrel jack. Don't order the "WSU090-2000-R" version, because its polarity is flipped.

docs.title: Regulator Choices
docs.text: Rail Choice Also considered Why +5V L7805CV (linear, 1.5 A) LM2940CT-5.0 (linear); R-78E5.0-1.0 (switching) It follows the course rule of using a linear regulator, gives about 3× the current I need, works with cheap capacitors, and is the cheapest. The full comparison is on my Component Selection page. +3.3V MIC5353 (built into the Nano, 500 mA) MCP1700-3302E/TO (250 mA) It already comes on the Curiosity Nano at no extra cost, and 500 mA is about 3× the 163 mA I need. Adding a separate regulator would only add parts and take up board space.

docs.title: Heat check (L7805CV)
docs.text:
Check Result Heat made: (9 V − 5 V) × 0.51 A + regulator's own use about 2.1 W Without a heatsink (50 °C/W) about 130 °C, too hot (limit 125 °C) With a TO-220 heatsink (25 °C/W or better) about 89 °C, safe

A linear regulator gets rid of the extra 4 V (9 V in, 5 V out) by turning it into heat. Without a heatsink it would get too hot at the worst case, so I will add a clip-on TO-220 heatsink. In normal use the speaker and alert LED are only on during a reminder, so most of the time it will run much cooler than this worst case.

docs.title: Calculated Battery Life
docs.text:
My hub board runs from the wall adapter, so it doesn't have a main battery. The only battery is the small coin cell that keeps the clock running when the adapter is unplugged.

Calculated Battery Life Component Name Part Number Supply Voltage Range Capacity (mAh) Required By RTC (mA) Unit RTC Backup Battery Panasonic CR2032 +3 V 225 0.0012 mA Battery Life 187,500 hours

187,500 hours is about 21 years. That is longer than the battery's shelf life of about 10 years, so the backup battery should last as long as the product does.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The 9 V input is above the 7 V the L7805CV needs to work (5 V out + 2 V it needs as extra).
  • The hub is one single board, so one power budget covers everything.
